name: Masala Dosa

ingredients.item: dosa batter (rice and urad dal, fermented)

steps: For the potato filling, heat oil in a pan, add mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add curry leaves and green chillies.
Add sliced onions and saute until translucent, then add turmeric powder.
Add mashed potatoes and salt, mix well, sprinkle a little water, and cook for 5 minutes until well combined; set the filling aside.
Heat a flat griddle (tawa) and lightly grease it, then wipe off excess oil with a cloth.
Pour a ladle of fermented dosa batter in the centre and spread it outward in a thin, even circular motion.
Drizzle a little oil around the edges and cook on medium heat until the base turns golden and crisp.
Place a portion of the potato filling in the centre of the dosa and fold it over into a half-moon or roll shape.
Serve immediately, hot and crisp, with coconut chutney and sambar.
tips: The batter must be well fermented and slightly bubbly for a naturally crisp, tangy dosa.

name: Plain Dosa
steps: Give the fermented batter a gentle stir and adjust consistency with a little water if it has thickened.
Heat a flat non-stick or cast iron griddle on medium-high heat until a drop of water sizzles on contact.
Lower the heat slightly, pour a ladle of batter in the centre, and spread it in outward circles to form a thin round.
Drizzle a little oil or ghee around the edges and on top.
Cook until the underside turns golden brown and crisp, and the edges start to lift naturally.
Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and remove from the griddle.
Serve immediately with coconut chutney and sambar.
tips: Keep the griddle at a consistent medium-high heat; too hot and the batter won't spread thinly, too cool and it won't crisp.

name: Idli

ingredients.item: idli batter (rice and urad dal, fermented)

steps: Grease the idli mould plates lightly with oil.
Give the fermented batter a gentle stir without deflating it too much.
Fill a boiler or steamer pot with water and bring it to a rolling boil.
Ladle the batter into each idli mould cavity, filling about three-quarters full.
Place the stand into the steamer, cover with a lid, and steam on medium-high heat for 10-12 minutes.
Check doneness by inserting a toothpick or spoon; it should come out clean.
Let the idlis rest for 2-3 minutes before demoulding with a wet spoon.
Serve hot with coconut chutney and sambar.
tips: Do not over-steam idlis as they can turn hard; check them from the 10-minute mark onward.

name: Medu Vada
steps: Soak urad dal for at least 3-4 hours, then drain well.
Grind the dal with minimal water into a thick, fluffy batter, and whip it by hand for a couple of minutes to add air.
Fold in chopped green chillies, ginger, curry leaves, peppercorns, cumin seeds and salt.
Heat oil in a deep pan to medium-hot.
Wet your hands, take a portion of batter, shape it into a doughnut with a hole in the centre, and gently slide it into the hot oil.
Fry on medium heat, turning occasionally, until golden brown and crisp on all sides, about 4-5 minutes per batch.
Drain on paper towels and serve hot with coconut chutney and sambar.
tips: The batter must be thick and well-aerated; a watery batter will absorb too much oil and won't hold its shape.

name: Sambar
steps: Pressure cook toor dal with turmeric and enough water until soft and mushy, about 15-20 minutes, then whisk smooth.
In a separate pot, cook the mixed vegetables in water until nearly tender.
Add tamarind pulp and sambar powder to the vegetables and simmer for 8-10 minutes.
Add the cooked dal to the vegetable mixture and simmer together for 10 minutes, adding water to adjust consistency.
Add salt and let the sambar simmer gently so all the flavours meld together.
In a small pan, heat oil, add mustard seeds, dried red chillies and curry leaves, and let them splutter.
Pour the tempering over the sambar and mix well.
Serve hot with idli, dosa or steamed rice.
tips: Fresh, good-quality sambar powder makes a big difference; toast it briefly in the tempering oil for extra aroma.

name: Rasam
steps: Dilute tamarind pulp in about 3 cups of water and add chopped tomatoes and rasam powder.
Bring this mixture to a boil and simmer for 10 minutes until the raw tamarind smell mellows.
Add the mashed cooked dal and salt, and simmer for another 5-7 minutes, adding water to adjust consistency.
In a small pan, heat ghee, add mustard seeds, cumin seeds, crushed garlic and curry leaves, and let them splutter.
Pour the tempering over the simmering rasam.
Let the rasam come to a single gentle boil (do not boil vigorously for long) and switch off the heat.
Garnish with fresh coriander and serve hot as a soup or over steamed rice.
tips: Rasam should only be brought to a light simmer at the end; over-boiling dulls its fresh tangy aroma.

name: Coconut Chutney
steps: Combine grated coconut, roasted chana dal, green chillies, ginger and salt in a blender.
Add a little water and grind into a smooth, thick paste, adjusting water for desired consistency.
Transfer the chutney to a serving bowl.
Heat oil in a small pan, add mustard seeds and curry leaves, and let them splutter.
Pour the tempering over the chutney and mix gently just before serving.
Serve alongside idli, dosa or vada.
tips: Use fresh, not desiccated, coconut for the best flavour and texture.

name: Uttapam
steps: Mix chopped onion, tomato, green chillies and coriander together in a bowl for topping.
Heat a griddle on medium heat and grease lightly.
Pour a ladleful of batter and spread it into a thick round, slightly thicker than a regular dosa.
Immediately sprinkle a generous portion of the vegetable topping over the batter and press gently with the back of a spoon so it sticks.
Drizzle oil around the edges and cook on medium-low heat until the base turns golden brown.
Flip carefully and cook the topping side for another 2 minutes.
Serve hot with coconut chutney and sambar.
tips: Cook uttapam on lower heat than dosa since it is thicker and needs more time to cook through.

name: Ven Pongal
steps: Dry roast moong dal lightly until fragrant, then wash it along with the rice.
Pressure cook rice and dal together with about 4 cups of water and salt until very soft and mushy, about 15 minutes.
Heat ghee in a small pan, add cashews and fry until golden, then remove and set aside.
In the same ghee, add cumin seeds, crushed peppercorns, chopped ginger and curry leaves, and let them sizzle.
Pour the tempering, along with the fried cashews, over the cooked rice and dal mixture.
Mix well, mashing slightly for a soft, porridge-like consistency, adding hot water if it seems too thick.
Serve hot with coconut chutney or sambar.
tips: Pongal should be soft and slightly mushy, not fluffy like regular cooked rice, so don't be shy with the water.

name: Upma
steps: Dry roast the semolina in a pan on medium heat until lightly golden and aromatic, then set aside.
In the same pan, heat oil and add mustard seeds and urad dal, letting them splutter and turn golden.
Add curry leaves, green chillies and chopped onion, and saute until the onion softens.
If using, add mixed vegetables and cook for 2-3 minutes until slightly tender.
Add about 2.5 cups of water and salt, and bring to a rolling boil.
Lower the heat and slowly stream in the roasted semolina while stirring continuously to avoid lumps.
Cover and cook on low heat for 3-4 minutes until all the water is absorbed and the upma is fluffy.
Serve hot with coconut chutney or a wedge of lemon.
tips: Roasting the semolina well beforehand prevents a raw, pasty taste in the final dish.

name: Bisi Bele Bath
steps: Pressure cook rice and toor dal together with plenty of water until very soft and well mashed.
In a separate pot, cook the mixed vegetables with tamarind pulp until nearly tender.
Add bisi bele bath powder to the vegetables and simmer for 8-10 minutes to cook out the raw spice taste.
Combine the cooked rice-dal mixture with the vegetable mixture, adding hot water to reach a thick, porridge-like consistency.
Simmer everything together for 10-12 minutes, stirring occasionally, and season with salt.
In a small pan, heat ghee, add mustard seeds, curry leaves and peanuts, and fry until the peanuts turn golden.
Pour the tempering over the bisi bele bath and mix well.
Serve hot with a side of raita, potato chips or papad.
tips: The dish should be thick and slightly loose, closer to a risotto than dry rice; add hot water gradually to get this consistency.

name: Curd Rice
steps: Mash the cooked rice slightly while still warm so it breaks down a little for a creamy texture.
Mix in milk and let the rice cool to room temperature.
Once cooled, add yogurt and salt, and mix well to a smooth, creamy consistency, adjusting with more yogurt or milk as needed.
Heat oil in a small pan, add mustard seeds and urad dal, and let them splutter and turn golden.
Add chopped green chillies, grated ginger and curry leaves, and saute for a few seconds.
Pour the tempering over the curd rice and mix gently.
Chill briefly if desired and serve with pickle or fried papad.
tips: Mixing warm rice with milk before adding yogurt keeps the curd rice creamy rather than watery once it sits.

name: Lemon Rice

ingredients.item: mustard seeds, urad dal and chana dal

steps: Heat oil in a pan and add mustard seeds, urad dal and chana dal, frying until the dals turn golden.
Add peanuts and fry until crunchy.
Add slit green chillies, curry leaves and turmeric powder, and saute for a few seconds.
Add the cooled cooked rice and salt, and gently toss to combine without mashing the grains.
Cook for 2-3 minutes on low heat to warm the rice through.
Turn off the heat and stir in fresh lemon juice, mixing well so it coats evenly.
Serve warm or at room temperature, garnished with coriander if desired.
tips: Using day-old, cooled rice prevents the dish from turning mushy or sticky.

name: Puliyodarai (Tamarind Rice)

ingredients.item: mustard seeds, urad dal and chana dal

steps: Dry roast sesame seeds and 2 dried red chillies separately until fragrant, cool, and grind into a coarse powder.
Heat sesame oil in a pan, add mustard seeds, urad dal, chana dal and remaining dried red chillies, frying until golden.
Add peanuts and curry leaves and fry until the peanuts turn crunchy.
Add the thick tamarind pulp, salt and a little jaggery, and simmer on low heat until it thickens into a jam-like paste, about 10-12 minutes.
Stir in the ground sesame-chilli powder and mix well.
Add the cooled cooked rice in batches, gently folding the tamarind paste through so every grain is coated.
Let it rest for 10-15 minutes for the flavours to develop before serving.
Serve at room temperature, garnished with a few extra peanuts.
tips: The tamarind paste base (puli kachal) can be made in a larger batch and refrigerated for quick tamarind rice anytime.

name: Rava Kesari
steps: Heat 2 tbsp ghee in a pan, fry cashews and raisins until golden, then remove and set aside.
In the same pan, add remaining ghee and roast the semolina on low-medium heat, stirring constantly, until fragrant and light golden, about 5-6 minutes.
In a separate pot, bring water to a boil with the food colour, if using.
Carefully pour the hot water into the roasted semolina while stirring continuously to avoid lumps.
Cook on low heat, stirring, until the semolina absorbs the water and thickens, about 3-4 minutes.
Add sugar and mix well; the mixture will loosen as the sugar melts, then thicken again as it cooks.
Stir in cardamom powder and the fried cashews and raisins, and cook for 2-3 more minutes until glossy.
Serve warm as a dessert or festive sweet.
tips: Always add hot water to hot roasted semolina to avoid lump formation.

name: Chettinad Chicken Curry
steps: Dry roast coriander seeds, fennel seeds, peppercorns and dried red chillies until aromatic, then cool.
Add grated coconut to the roasted spices and grind into a coarse, slightly textured masala paste with a little water.
Heat oil in a heavy pot, add curry leaves and chopped onions, and saute until golden brown.
Add ginger garlic paste and cook for a minute, then add chopped tomatoes and cook until soft.
Add the ground Chettinad masala paste and cook for 5-6 minutes until the raw smell disappears and oil begins to separate.
Add chicken pieces and salt, and mix well to coat in the masala.
Cover and cook on medium-low heat for 20-25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is tender and the gravy thickens.
Garnish with curry leaves and serve hot with steamed rice or dosa.
tips: Freshly dry-roasting and grinding the spice blend, rather than using pre-made powder, is key to authentic Chettinad flavour.

name: Gongura Chicken
steps: Wash gongura leaves well and cook them in a little water until wilted and soft, then blend into a coarse puree.
Heat oil in a pot, add curry leaves and chopped onions, and saute until golden.
Add ginger garlic paste and cook for a minute.
Add chicken pieces, turmeric, chilli powder and salt, and mix well to coat.
Cook covered on medium heat for 10 minutes until the chicken releases some juices.
Add the gongura puree and mix well, then cover and cook for 15-20 minutes until the chicken is tender and the gravy thickens.
Adjust salt considering the natural tang of the gongura, and simmer for a final 3-4 minutes.
Serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Gongura is naturally sour, so taste before adding extra salt or any souring agent.

name: South Indian Vegetable Kurma
steps: Grind grated coconut, fried gram, green chillies and fennel seeds with a little water into a smooth paste.
Heat oil in a pot and saute chopped onions until translucent.
Add chopped tomato and cook until soft.
Add mixed vegetables and a little water, cover, and cook until the vegetables are nearly tender, about 10-12 minutes.
Add the ground coconut paste and salt, and mix well.
Simmer on low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the gravy thickens slightly and the vegetables are fully cooked.
Adjust consistency with water as needed; the kurma should be medium-thick.
Serve hot with idiyappam, dosa or chapati.
tips: Do not boil vigorously after adding the coconut paste, as it can cause the gravy to separate.

name: Mysore Pak
steps: Sift the gram flour twice to remove lumps and set aside.
Melt the ghee and keep it warm on very low heat nearby.
In a heavy pan, combine sugar and water and cook until it reaches a one-string consistency syrup.
Reduce heat to low and gradually add the sifted gram flour into the syrup, wielding a whisk continuously to avoid lumps.
Add a ladle of hot ghee and keep stirring; the mixture will bubble and start to loosen.
Continue adding ghee gradually while stirring vigorously, alternating between mixture thickening and loosening, for about 12-15 minutes.
When the mixture starts leaving the sides of the pan and turns porous with visible bubbles, immediately pour it into a greased tray.
Let it cool for a few minutes, score into squares while still warm, and let it set fully before cutting through and serving.
tips: Work quickly and confidently once the mixture starts to set, as Mysore Pak firms up fast and timing is crucial.

name: Pesarattu
steps: Soak whole green moong dal and rice together for at least 4 hours.
Drain and grind with green chillies, ginger, cumin seeds and salt into a smooth, pourable batter, adding water as needed.
Heat a griddle on medium-high heat and grease lightly.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread it into a thin round, similar to a dosa.
Sprinkle finely chopped onion over the batter and press gently.
Drizzle oil around the edges and cook until the base turns golden and crisp, then flip briefly to cook the other side.
Fold and serve hot with ginger chutney or coconut chutney.
tips: Unlike dosa batter, this one does not need fermentation, so it can be made fresh the same day after a few hours of soaking.

name: Coconut Rice

ingredients.item: mustard seeds, urad dal and chana dal

steps: Heat oil in a pan and add mustard seeds, urad dal and chana dal, frying until golden.
Add dried red chillies, curry leaves and cashews, and fry until the cashews turn golden.
Add the grated coconut and saute for 2-3 minutes on low heat until lightly fragrant, being careful not to brown it.
Add the cooled cooked rice and salt, and gently toss everything together until well combined.
Cook for 2-3 minutes on low heat to warm through without making the rice sticky.
Serve warm or at room temperature, garnished with extra curry leaves if desired.
tips: Sauteing the coconut only briefly keeps its flavour fresh and prevents it from turning bitter.
